transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-25
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jonah Patel (Redwood SE), Mark Landry (Polaris Eng Lead), Sarah Kim (Polaris CTO), Tina Lopez (Polaris DevOps), Evan Ortiz (Polaris ML)

Summary:
Polaris is evaluating Redwood for an onramp integration that supports an initial hosted deployment then a transition to Dedicated or Private (VPC) for regulatory traffic. Primary goals: low-latency chat endpoints, LangChain/LlamaIndex integration for retrieval-augmented generation, gateway/proxy pattern to front Redwood for internal microservices, and per-team rate limits/quotas plus observability hooks (traces, token cost breakdowns). They requested pilot scope, pricing, and a short integration guide.

Topics:
- Hosting mode strategy: hosted -> dedicated/private
- SDKs + LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter patterns
- Gateway/proxy recommendations and sidecar vs central proxy tradeoffs
- Rate limiting, API keys, quotas, and tenant isolation
- Observability: traces, token-level cost, log retention, hooks for SLOs
- Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, VPC peering, audit logs

[00:00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we've got about 55 minutes, we'll go through what you want to achieve and then Priya will walk the technical approach. quick intros?

[00:00:12] Mark Landry: sure, Mark here, eng lead at Polaris. we're building an internal assistant for our ops and sales teams, want safe rollout and predictable cost.

[00:00:20] Sarah Kim: Sarah, CTO. main ask is we can't have PII leave our VPC for some workloads and we need strong audit trails.

[00:00:28] Alex Chen: great, thanks — Priya over to you to cover the integration shapes.

[00:00:33] Priya Nair: hey all, yeah so at a high level Redwood supports three modes, hosted api for quick launch, dedicated reserved pools for steady throughput, and private for VPC/onprem. for integration patterns we see two common flows — direct SDK integration in app services, or a gateway/proxy that fronts Redwood so you can centralize auth, rate limits, caching.

[00:01:05] Jonah Patel: (interject) and we have LangChain and LlamaIndex helpers in the SDK so you don't need to rewire a lot of code. sample adapters are in the repo, but I'll show a quick snippet after.

[00:01:18] Mark Landry: quick Q — we use LangChain heavily, but also have an internal retriever. what does the adapter look like? do we push embeddings to Redwood or keep vector store internal?

[00:01:30] Priya Nair: good question. most customers keep their vector store (e.g., Pinecone, FAISS, internal S3-backed) and call Redwood for generation only. we support passing embeddings as part of the context and also offer embeddings API if you want to centralize. for RAG with LlamaIndex there's a lightweight connector that marshals retrieved docs into the prompt template; we can share an example that uses your retriever.

[00:01:58] Tina Lopez: so in the pilot we'd likely keep vectors internal for control, yes. another question: rate limiting per team and per-route — can Redwood enforce quotas per API key and per route?

[00:02:11] Alex Chen: yes, Redwood supports per-token billing breakdowns and per-key rate limits, plus quotas. you can configure soft and hard limits, and we support webhook notifications on quota events. for Dedicated you also get more granular policies.

[00:02:28] Evan Ortiz: is burst capacity automatic? our traffic is spiky — mornings and end-of-month reports.

[00:02:33] Priya Nair: hosted has burst windows but if you need predictable spike capacity and SLOs we'd recommend Dedicated with burst pockets. if you're on Private we can do autoscaling within your VPC but it depends on your infra.

[00:02:47] Sarah Kim: about the gateway — we're debating sidecar per service vs central proxy. what are tradeoffs from a Redwood perspective?

[00:02:56] Priya Nair: sidecar gives you per-service observability and retries local caching; central proxy simplifies routing, consolidated auth, and makes it easier to A/B route between hosted and dedicated. many teams do a hybrid — central gateway that forwards to a sidecar for latency-sensitive workflows. note: KV cache was mentioned as important — our runtime uses KV cache for decoder state; sometimes that gets transcribed as K V cash in older transcripts, so don't worry — it's the same KV cache.

[00:03:28] Mark Landry: (laughs) fair. about observability hooks — we need request traces stitched into our existing tracing (Jaeger/OpenTelemetry) and token-level cost per request. is that possible?

[00:03:40] Jonah Patel: yes, Redwood has tracing headers and an OTLP export option for many deployments. we also surface a token breakdown per request in the console and via API so you can correlate cost to traces. retention windows are configurable; hosted has default retention but enterprises can request longer retention as an add-on.

[00:04:00] Tina Lopez: do you push logs to our S3 or does Redwood store them? we need to keep audit logs on our side for 7 years for compliance.

[00:04:09] Priya Nair: for Private deployments you control where logs live. for Hosted we can push logs via secure transfer to your S3 or set up log forwarding to your SIEM. we also support long-term audit export. there's sometimes nuance around PII redaction — we offer automatic redaction rules and also allow customer-side post-processing.

[00:04:27] Sarah Kim: KMS and key management — can we use our own KMS/HSM?

[00:04:32] Alex Chen: yes, Dedicated and Private support customer-managed keys. Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer KMS for certain enterprise tiers. we'll add specifics in the security pack.

[00:04:41] Mark Landry: let's talk throughput and sizing — our baseline is about 10k requests/day with 150 tokens average per request, peak qps ~45. what instance types and cost profile should we expect?

[00:04:54] Priya Nair: for that profile hosted is fine for pilot. Dedicated pools for that QPS are typically a mix of A100/RTX-class GPUs depending on model; cost depends on token mix and batching. we'll run a quick bench if you share a sample traffic CSV — the bench will show latency p50/p95 and token cost estimates.

[00:05:15] Evan Ortiz: what about quantized models? we might want to use 4-bit variants to cut cost. any issues with compatibility for LlamaIndex?

[00:05:23] Jonah Patel: we support quantized variants; LlamaIndex and LangChain don't care about quantization as long as model API semantics are the same. some edge cases around function calling and structured outputs need validation — we'll surface those in the examples.

[00:05:36] Tina Lopez: can we shadow traffic to Redwood from prod? like send a copy for evaluation without impacting latency?

[00:05:42] Priya Nair: yes — shadowing and canary are supported. we also have a request-forking option in the gateway so you can route to Redwood plus your internal model. shadowed requests don't count towards quotas in pilot setups if we configure test tenants.

[00:06:00] Mark Landry: on auth patterns, we use SSO (SAML) internally and want RBAC on who can call specific templates. can Redwood integrate with our IAM?

[00:06:08] Alex Chen: Redwood supports SAML/SCIM for user provisioning, and RBAC on the console and API keys. For more granular route-level auth you can put Redwood behind your gateway and enforce claims.

[00:06:20] Sarah Kim: any known gotchas for using Redwood SDK with existing LangChain agents?

[00:06:25] Jonah Patel: the main thing is to check streaming semantics. LangChain streaming wrappers assume a chunking pattern; our SDK supports streaming chunk events and also offers an adapter that translates between streams and LangChain's callback manager. some older LangChain versions have mismatch on error retry semantics so we provide a compatibility snippet.

[00:06:44] Priya Nair: I'll send a repo link with LangChain + LlamaIndex short examples: retrieval -> prompt -> Redwood generation -> parse structured output. that should reduce integration time.

[00:06:55] Tina Lopez: observability again — we want per-route SLO alerts when token cost spikes. can we create custom alerts from Redwood or need to route to our Alerting tool?

[00:07:03] Alex Chen: Redwood Console supports per-route thresholds and alerting for errors/latency/cost. you can also forward metrics to your existing monitoring (Prometheus/Grafana) and wire alerts there. many customers prefer native quick alerts + external long-term alerting.

[00:07:18] Mark Landry: security review timeline — we typically do a SOC2 questionnaire and then a deeper compliance review. what materials can you share?

[00:07:25] Alex Chen: we'll share SOC2 report (redacted), our security whitepaper, VPC networking diagrams, KMS/HSM integration docs, and the data processing addendum. Priya will include the network flow diagram for Private deployments.

[00:07:40] Evan Ortiz: any SLA numbers we can expect for Dedicated?

[00:07:44] Priya Nair: Dedicated comes with uptime SLA and latency guardrails; we can share the exact SLOs in the SOW. Hosted has best-effort but historically strong 99.x availability; Dedicated is for guaranteed throughput.

[00:07:57] Jonah Patel: quick demo idea — we could push a tiny sample to show LangChain retrieval + Redwood generation in 20 minutes during the pilot kickoff.

[00:08:07] Sarah Kim: that'd be helpful. also curious about cost control — can we pin model versions to avoid silent regressions?

[00:08:14] Alex Chen: yes, version pinning is supported; you can pin to exact model builds and we have rollout policies (canary, A/B) with automatic fallback to previous version if metrics regress.

[00:08:26] Tina Lopez: rate limit enforcement detail: do you throttle with 429s or queue? we prefer soft queuing to reduce client error handling complexity.

[00:08:33] Priya Nair: by default we return 429 for hard limits, but soft limits can be configured to queue or apply backpressure at the gateway. Dedicated gives more configurability. We can include sample configs.

[00:08:48] Mark Landry: how about request signing and payload validation? we need tamper-proof logs.

[00:08:53] Alex Chen: we support signed requests in the Private deployment and HMAC style keys for Hosted. Audit logs include request hashes and you can store your own signed copies if needed.

[00:09:05] Evan Ortiz: do you have examples of teams that did a hosted->dedicated migration? what's the typical friction?

[00:09:12] Jonah Patel: yes, we've done migrations for a few mid-market customers. friction points: ensuring identical model variant (quantization parity), tuning batching/latency settings, and adjusting monitoring dashboards. we provide a migration checklist and we often run a parallel Dedicated environment during the transition.

[00:09:29] Mark Landry: OK, pilot scope — what do you recommend for a 4-week pilot to validate RAG and latency?

[00:09:36] Priya Nair: 4-week pilot: week 0 setup + security review, week 1 integrate LangChain examples and run smoke tests, week 2 run synthetic traffic and shadow prod, week 3 run bench and fine-tune batching/kv cache settings, final week wrap + decision. deliverables: bench report, SLO table, cost estimate, and integration notes.

[00:09:57] Sarah Kim: fine. timeline-wise we're targetting Q1 rollouts but want pilot done by mid-December.

[00:10:03] Alex Chen: sounds doable. we'll send the SOW and pilot checklist.

[00:10:08] Tina Lopez: one operational question — does Redwood support per-customer tenanting within a single Dedicated pool? we have multiple internal teams with isolation needs.

[00:10:17] Priya Nair: yes, Dedicated supports logical tenancy and quotas per team. for strict isolation you can provide separate Dedicated pools per team. We can show cost tradeoffs.

[00:10:28] Jonah Patel: also, if you want to do model canaries per team we support per-route model routing so teams can test different model versions without affecting others.

[00:10:38] Mark Landry: any limitations on prompt size and streaming when using your SDK vs raw HTTP?

[00:10:44] Priya Nair: SDK and HTTP are feature parity; streaming works similarly. prompt size limits depend on model variant; we'll put specific token limits for the models you want in the bench output.

[00:10:56] Sarah Kim: final security bump — do you do annual pen tests and will you share results?

[00:11:02] Alex Chen: yes, we do regular penetration testing and can share summaries. we'll include contact for security team.

[00:11:10] Mark Landry: okay, good. any other blockers from your side?

[00:11:14] Tina Lopez: not right now. Mark will collect compliance contacts and the traffic sample.

[00:11:20] Alex Chen: awesome. Jonah, can you recap the technical artifacts you'll send?

[00:11:24] Jonah Patel: sure — LangChain + LlamaIndex examples wired to Redwood SDK, gateway proxy config snippets (sidecar and central), sample rate-limit configs, tracing header examples, and a short bench script.

[00:11:36] Priya Nair: and I'll attach the security pack: SOC2 doc, network flow diagrams, KMS notes.

[00:11:42] Alex Chen: I'll follow up with pricing and a draft pilot SOW. target dates: pricing by 2027-11-29, examples by 2027-11-30, pilot kickoff week 2027-12-06. does that calendar work?

[00:11:55] Sarah Kim: yes that's fine.

[00:11:58] Mark Landry: works for us.

[00:12:02] Alex Chen: great — last thing: do you have any concerns about vendor lock-in or model drift?

[00:12:08] Evan Ortiz: model drift yes — we want to be able to swap model backends if quality changes.

[00:12:12] Priya Nair: Redwood supports routing rules so you can fallback to alternate models or your in-house model. we also provide eval hooks and regression alerts tied to a prompt set so you get notified when outputs degrade.

[00:12:26] Sarah Kim: OK, thanks everyone. let's capture next steps.

Action items (captured earlier):
- Alex: pricing + SOW (due 2027-11-29)
- Priya: LangChain/LlamaIndex + security pack (due 2027-11-30)
- Mark: sample traffic + compliance contacts (due 2027-11-30)

[00:12:50] Alex Chen: unless there are more questions we'll wrap. thanks for your time.

[00:12:55] Mark Landry: thanks, appreciate it.

[00:12:58] Jonas? (crosstalk)

[00:13:00] Jonah Patel: thanks all, will follow up in the thread.

End transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (K V cash / KV cache), speaker overlap toward the end.
